title: Teachers Need Time to Learn about Using Time
author: Dave Stuart Jr.
summary: Drawing on his own early-career overwork, Stuart argues that schools should treat time-management as a subject for site-based professional development rather than leaving it to individual willpower, framing teacher overwork as a systemic driver of disengagement and attrition rather than just a personal failing. He outlines three principles: prizing results over hours worked, citing Morten Hansen's finding that productivity actually declines once workers exceed 65 hours per week; starting from time constraints rather than task lists, invoking Parkinson's Law and Cal Newport's fixed-schedule productivity system; and "satisficing" most tasks while reserving maximizing effort for the few that matter most, drawing on Herbert Simon's economic theory and Barry Schwartz's research linking maximizing tendencies to lower happiness. He calls on school leaders to model vulnerability and psychological safety around these principles using Daniel Coyle's framework for building effective cultures. The piece closes autobiographically, with Stuart noting he left teaching after three overworked years before returning armed with these principles.
points: Stuart reframes teacher time-management as a professional-development gap rather than a personal-discipline failure, citing overwork as "a leading cause of teacher disengagement and attrition" at the system level.
Morten Hansen's research on 5,000+ professionals found productivity actually declines once workers exceed 65 hours per week, undercutting the "more hours equals more impact" teaching mythology.

Constraints should precede task selection: fixed-schedule productivity (Cal Newport) and Parkinson's Law both suggest that limiting available hours forces genuine prioritization instead of endless task accumulation.

Herbert Simon's "satisficing" concept — completing most tasks at the lowest acceptable quality to protect capacity for the few that matter most — is offered as a practical antidote to the maximizing tendencies Barry Schwartz's research links to lower happiness.
quotes: The thing is, teacher overwork isn't a laughing matter. While perhaps humorous at the individual level, at the system level it is a leading cause of teacher disengagement and attrition.
The professional's objective is to do her work with ever-improving levels of excellence. She aims at results for her students, not clocking hours for herself.

In fact, Hansen finds that once a worker reaches 65 hours per week, there is a decrease in overall productivity — so in terms of our jobs in education, we produce worse classroom learning outcomes when we work 70 hours than we do when we work 60.
As Cyril Northcote Parkinson once famously quipped, the work that we have to do will always expand to fill the time that we give it.

Nobel prizewinner Herbert Simon identified that while the tendency in organizations often tends toward maximizing — toward completing tasks at the optimal level of quality — it is often best to satisfice — to complete tasks at the lowest level of acceptable quality — for the sake of maximizing on the few tasks that matter most.

For example, in one 2002 study, the researchers found that people who tend toward maximizing are less likely to be happy, more likely to suffer from upward social comparison (a common struggle, especially for novice teachers), and less likely to be satisfied with consumer decisions.

As it turned out, that early career teacher who I started this article with didn't last for very long. After my third year teaching and with starting a family on the horizon, I did what many sane people do: I left.
